pr_title: _thread: fix a race condition when running garbage collection from multiple threads
pr_comments:
Thanks for the fix, it does look sensible, to not release the GC mutex in the middle of `gc_alloc()`.

But did you find a case where `gc_alloc()` was interrupted by another thread between unlocking the mutex and then calling `gc_collect()`?  I think that allocation and garbage collection are independent and it should in theory be possible to switch to another thread in between these calls.

[Python code](https://pastebin.com/PTD0qE8U), compiled with DEBUG=1 can reproduce the issue. After the patch, the issue is not reproducible with the code above. So yes, I think there is a race  when `gc_alloc()` is interrupted by another thread when unlocking the mutex and then calling `gc_collect().` 
Note: compiling with DEBUG=1 is not necessary, but helps increase the chances of reproducing the issue faster

I took a detailed look at this bug.  I was able to reproduce the problem on unix x86-64, with both the standard and coverage builds.  It seems easier to trigger the bug on the standard build.  The bug is much easier to trigger by putting a lot of `sched_yield()` calls (eg 100 of them) just after the call to gc_collect() in the for-ever loop in gc_alloc.  This forces other threads to take the gc_mutex, making the bug appear.

While the PR here does fix it, the bug is also fixed by #4044.  See the comment there for an explanation of the cause of the bug.

@mzakharocsc thanks very much for providing the test case to help make this bug reproducible.  It would be good to include that test (possibly simplified a bit) in the test suite here.  Would you mind if I took it and used it?

It might also be good to take the part of this PR that moves the finaliser stuff up a bit in gc_alloc, because that is a neat optimisation.

Yes, you can use the test program as you see fit. 
One could still argue that releasing GC mutex between alloc and gc_collect() and then acquiring it again is not the best idea in terms of performance, needless lock/unlock, needless (possible) context switch, etc. Why not keep it all atomic? Yes, API gets a bit hairy, but maybe we can get around that somehow?

> One could still argue that releasing GC mutex between alloc and gc_collect() and then acquiring it again is not the best idea in terms of performance,

I agree.  (Although it could be argued that it is good to release the mutex to let the other threads make some progress, but in this case it's not because the only thing the other threads would be blocked on would be entry to malloc/realloc/free which they should stay blocked on until the current thread finishes the collection and allocation.)

> Yes, API gets a bit hairy, but maybe we can get around that somehow?

It would be good to find a way to make it tidy, especially since a fair few ports don't use threading and so shouldn't need to worry about this lock/unlock.

issue_context.title: Threading using _thread causes  segmentation fault, AttributeError:
issue_context.body:
My micropython [program](https://pastebin.com/PTD0qE8U) is using queues and _thread API to schedule processing across multiple cores. It crashes with segfaults, or error messages like these:

> AttributeError: 'Bar' object has no attribute 'lock'
> Segmentation fault (core dumped)

or this:
> ../../py/gc.c:575: gc_free: Assertion `ATB_GET_KIND(block) == AT_HEAD' failed.

or  this:
> ../../py/gc.c:673: gc_realloc: Assertion `ATB_GET_KIND(block) == AT_HEAD' failed.


It sometimes takes hours, and sometimes minutes to run the program and experience a crash. Errors are not consistent, switching between AttributeError, gc_free Assertion, or a quiet segfault. Any suggestions on how to attempt to resolve this would be much appreciated. 

Micropython version: 1.9.4. Target: unix  (8-core x86-64 and 4-core ARM).  My ARM setup seems to reproduce this more often than x86. Also, compiling with DEBUG=1 increases the probability of occurrence
comments:
I can imagine two possible causes:
* The memory allocator (py/gc.c) doesn't do proper locking.
* There is a memory corruption issue somewhere else.

See:
https://github.com/micropython/micropython/blob/master/py/gc.c#L99
Is the GIL enabled or disabled in your case?  If you are using the standard unix configuration then the answer would be that the GIL is disabled.
Information is missing to reproduce/debug the issue. Please provide the requested details, or we will have to close the issue.

review_comments: It's probably safer to put these GC_ENTER/GC_EXIT pairs in the `gc_collect()` implementation, because `gc_collect()` may be called by C code from another location, see eg https://github.com/micropython/micropython/blob/master/lib/utils/pyexec.c#L141
How do we best accomplish that? gc_collect() is used inside gc_alloc(), and we cannot release GC mutex without a segfaulty race.
maybe we rename the funciton to _gc_collect() in all the ports, and create a macro gc_collect(), which has GC_ENTER/EXIT wrapped around it?
